item.title: How calcium channels in muscle cells open together
item.description: Every step we take begins with a burst of calcium inside our muscle cells, causing them to contract. To prepare for action, the cells keep calcium locked in an internal compartment, the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Studding its membrane are thousands of RyR1 channels—the largest known ion channels—that contain pores that release the calcium. For a muscle to contract properly, RyR1 channels must open synchronously via a mechanism known as "coupled gating." How they accomplish this has been unclear since it was described almost 30 years ago. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: JWST finds early galaxies were already seeding the universe with heavy elements
item.description: When the universe was still in its infancy—only 500 million years after the Big Bang, or about 3% of its current age—some of the universe's earliest stars and galaxies had already formed. Astronomers have long predicted that much of the gas surrounding these young galaxies must have remained relatively pristine, composed mostly of hydrogen and helium, the primordial ingredients available in the newborn cosmos. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bay Area wastewater plants could nearly halve nitrogen cleanup costs by coordinating upgrades
item.description: Treating polluted water flowing into San Francisco Bay to meet regulatory requirements is going to cost ratepayers money. Exactly how much depends, in large part, on whether the region's wastewater treatment plant operators are willing and able to coordinate infrastructure construction and operation to meet these requirements, according to a Stanford University study published in Nature Water. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Anthropic touts AI-led biology discovery
item.description: U.S. artificial intelligence startup Anthropic on Wednesday unveiled the first discovery from its molecular biology lab, a previously unknown enzyme system spotted by its Claude model and touted by the company as proof that AI can speed up basic research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Alarm bells sound in Brussels as EU sales of Chinese hybrid cars rocket
item.description: Explosive growth in imported vehicles omitted from EV tariffs fuels concern for future of European carmakers EU imports three times more from China than bloc exports there Business news – live updates Sales of Chinese hybrid cars have rocketed in the EU in the past four and a half years, new data shows, underlining growing concerns in Brussels over the future of the European car industry. In 2022, just 659 Chinese-made fully hybrid cars (vehicles in which the petrol or diesel engine charge the motor and battery) were sold in the EU. However, after Brussels imposed anti-subsidy tariffs on… Fuente: The Guardian - World.

item.title: Archaeological 'breakthrough' could confirm origins of Paris
item.description: An ancient wall discovered in central Paris was hailed as a "major breakthrough" on Wednesday, as the archaeological find may have settled a long-standing debate about the location of the city's original settlement. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Record participation in ESA’s Industry Space Days 2026
item.description: On 16–17 September, the European Space Agency (ESA) hosted a record 3100 visitors from Europe’s space industry for a two-day Industry Space Days (ISD) event at ESA’s ESTEC technical centre in the Netherlands. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.description: Sean Gunn has proclaimed himself “retired” from doing the on-set motion capture for the fan-favorite “Guardians of the Galaxy” character Rocket Raccoon. item.title: Cloudy Cloak Over the Northwest
item.description: A low-lying cloud layer brought autumn ambience to western Washington and Oregon, while mountainous areas near the coast remained above the pall. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Aerial maps reveal successful woodland expansion in Scotland's Cairngorms
item.description: A University of Cambridge–led team has used aerial surveys across a huge swath of the Cairngorms National Park in Scotland to create detailed 3D maps that show the beginnings of large-scale recovery of native woodland. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: More REM sleep linked to lower risk of 83 diseases
item.description: A large study tracking more than 95,000 people suggests that how you sleep may be linked to your risk of developing dozens of diseases. People who spent more time in REM sleep had lower risks of 83 conditions, including dementia, heart failure, and Parkinson’s disease, while more deep sleep was associated with lower risks of conditions such as type 2 diabetes and major depression. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Fit, thin, curvy and toned: The contradictory body ideals young NZ women face online
item.description: For countless people, social media has become a go-to source of advice on how to look, eat and exercise. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: GLP-1 weight loss and diabetes drugs linked to nutritional deficiencies in nearly 1 in 6 children
item.description: Children taking GLP-1 medications (such as Victoza, Saxenda, Trulicity, and Ozempic) for weight loss, prediabetes, or type 2 diabetes may face an overlooked risk: nutritional deficiencies. A new study found that nearly 1 in 6 young patients developed a diagnosed deficiency within a year of starting treatment, with vitamin D deficiency affecting about 12%. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Study reveals how communication sequence strengthens green persuasion
item.description: The impact of sustainability messages may depend not only on their content but also on the order in which they are presented. The emotional response created by one message may influence how people interpret the next message about green initiatives. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: ‘Hanging on by a thread’: 11th hour decision to protect endangered birds from SA space project plans welcomed
item.description: The Eyre peninsula site is ‘precious and important’ habitats for southern emu-wren and home to 80% of the mallee whipbird population Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Conservation groups have welcomed an 11th-hour decision to protect “precious and important habitat” on South Australia’s Eyre peninsula from plans for a rocket launching facility. The Whalers Way “orbital launch complex”, which could see as many as 42 rockets a year take off from conservation land, had already been approved under federal and state planning and environment laws. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.
item.dc:creator: Petra Stock

item.title: A broken rib from the world’s largest T. rex hid a 66-million-year-old secret
item.description: A broken rib from Scotty, the largest known T. rex skeleton, contains an extraordinary fossilized network of blood vessels formed while the dinosaur was healing. Scientists used neutron and X-ray imaging to look inside the 66-million-year-old bone without damaging it, revealing details rarely preserved in fossils. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Acute hunger could reach 8 million children in six African countries as El Niño looms
item.description: About 8 million children across East and Southern Africa could face acute hunger by early 2027, a rise of 30%, as one of the strongest El Niño weather events in recent years fuels a growing food crisis, according to a new analysis by Save the Children. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Across southwest China and Thailand, plant turnover and nematode body width help explain soil diversity
item.description: Soils harbor some of the most diverse life on Earth. Soil nematodes play crucial roles in maintaining ecosystem functions. Yet how their diversity changes across large landscapes, and what drives those changes, remains poorly understood. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why AI won't fix Britain's supply chains
item.description: Businesses hoping AI will solve their supply chain problems risk wasting their investment unless they first fix weaknesses in their data, skills and management, according to new research published in the Benchmarking: An International Journal. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The “big one” might not come alone: Two major West Coast faults may strike back to back
item.description: The Cascadia subduction zone and northern San Andreas fault may sometimes rupture in rapid succession, according to evidence preserved in 3,100 years of ocean sediments. Researchers identified unusual sediment layers suggesting that earthquakes on the two systems have occurred just minutes to hours apart, including around the massive Cascadia earthquake of 1700. If such synchronization happened again, several major West Coast cities could face emergencies at nearly the same time. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Self-driving lab automates semiconductor ink synthesis and thin-film characterization
item.description: Developing new functional materials often requires testing numerous material combinations. Conventional experiments reach their limits quickly when many variants must be compared. To overcome this bottleneck, the new Energy Materials Acceleration Platform (E-MAP) at KIT automates key lab steps. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The stories we tell ourselves shape who we are
item.description: "One way or another, we are living the stories planted knowingly or unknowingly in us early in life, the stories that give our lives meaning."—Ben Okri, A Way of Being Free Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Por qué no hay mujeres en Artemis III: la explicación del astronauta Luca Parmitano
item.description: El astronauta de la Agencia Espacial Europea es uno de los cuatro integrantes de la nueva delegación; bromeó con la posibilidad de llevar comida de su país al espacio Fuente: La Nación - El Mundo.

item.title: Crown-of-thorns starfish can help reefs thrive
item.description: Crown-of-thorns starfish (COTS) are infamous in the marine world. Their toxin-loaded thorns give them a menacing appearance, and they have a reputation as destroyers of coral reefs. New research from the University of Sydney challenges the perception of COTS as purely destructive. The findings suggest controlled populations can have a positive impact on coral prevalence and diversity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: GenAI use among online adult learners associated with academic performance and technology confidence
item.description: University of Phoenix scholars have published research examining how nontraditional undergraduate students use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in online higher education. The study found that more frequent GenAI use was significantly associated with higher academic performance and stronger confidence in technology skills. Lower confidence in reading, writing and math, and greater time demands from work, study or family responsibilities, did not significantly predict use. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How lawyers can better support clients living with dementia
item.description: Lawyers play a critical role in helping people with dementia plan for the future. A recent study identifies knowledge gaps in the legal profession and key capabilities needed to better support people with dementia. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Astrophysicists use wave simulations to open a new window on dark matter
item.description: Astrophysicists from The University of Hong Kong (HKU), working with a research team led by Beijing Normal University (BNU), have developed a more physically realistic approach to testing how ultralight, or "fuzzy," dark matter could influence gravitationally lensed images. The study is the first to make gravitational-lensing predictions directly from three-dimensional wave simulations of fuzzy dark matter. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Biologists battle over North America's largest crayfish
item.description: When Caitlin Bloomer wrestled the massive Crawzilla crawdad—yes, that's its actual common name—out of the muck during a biological survey in Kentucky, she was convinced it was the largest crayfish ever recorded. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists make progress in mapping chemicals to six groups of common diseases
item.description: Exposure to hazardous chemicals can contribute to noncommunicable diseases and remains a key public health challenge. Most chemicals used in consumer products, including food packaging, lack sufficient data to determine whether they are safe. Current testing approaches cannot effectively check for all possible health outcomes, and many testing requirements check only for genotoxicity and examine one substance at a time. Yet evidence shows that consumers are simultaneously exposed to complex mixtures of chemicals from many types of products. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Can this biotech innovation halt the destructive march of a cereal killer?
item.description: A UK-led research collaboration has taken a significant step in the global effort to protect cereal crops from the devastating blast fungus. Researchers at the John Innes Centre explored a recently discovered class of plant defense receptors, showing at the molecular level how they limit blast pathogen attacks and how they might be bioengineered to provide broader, more durable immunity in wheat, barley and rice. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Combined satellite views offer clues to magma movement beneath Ethiopia's volcanoes
item.description: Magma moving beneath a volcano can make the ground rise, sink or shift sideways. Measuring these changes gives scientists clues about where magma is stored and how it travels. A study published in Geodesy and Geodynamics used satellite radar to examine the November 2025 eruption of Hayli Gubbi in Ethiopia's Afar Depression. Hayli Gubbi and nearby Erta Ale are separate volcanoes within the same volcanic zone, where three tectonic plates are pulling apart. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Dr. Paul Nestadt is about as steeped in suicide prevention as a person can be. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bennu asteroid samples point to a surprising origin involving Jupiter
item.description: The asteroid Bennu orbits the sun once every 1.2 years and approaches Earth every six years, passing within around 300,000 kilometers. NASA took advantage of this to collect material from the celestial body. In a spectacular operation in 2023, the US space agency collected samples from the surface of the asteroid Bennu by its OSIRIS-REx probe. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hervey Bay's dugongs make positive start on slow road to recovery
item.description: A small but positive increase in the number of dugongs spotted in coastal areas in south-east Queensland has researchers feeling cautiously optimistic about the vulnerable marine mammal achieving population revival. Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.title: Can the US and China verify an AI deal? Start-ups are starting to build the tools
item.description: There are growing calls for Washington and Beijing to agree to slow down development of artificial intelligence. But even if they wanted to do so, how could they verify that the other side would do the same? A group of researchers and start-ups is developing technology intended to make this a possibility, without relying on trust alone. Their proposed tools would allow third parties and governments to check some claims about how AI models are being trained or used – possibly without needing... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Vincent Chow

item.title: Starch-based sensor changes color to indicate moisture in food packaging
item.description: Brazilian researchers have developed a biodegradable, starch-based sensor that changes color when moisture enters food packaging. With the addition of cobalt chloride, the sensor changes from blue to pink as moisture levels rise and back to blue as they fall. Consumers and manufacturers could use it to monitor the quality and crispness of foods such as cookies with the naked eye or a cellphone camera, without complex equipment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Gene editing produces soybean with more than 90% oleic acid
item.description: Sejong University researchers have developed a high-quality soybean with improved oxidative stability, reduced saturated fat and increased seed fatty acid content. The research team led by Hyun Uk Kim, a professor in the Department of Bio-Industrial Resources Engineering at Sejong University, created the soybean line containing up to 90.2% oleic acid using CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing technology. The study is published in the Plant Biotechnology Journal. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Modernizes Commercial Airline Systems
item.description: NASA’s researchers know that when you settle into your seat on a commercial flight, you expect a smooth takeoff, views over the clouds, a steady descent, and hopefully an early arrival at your destination. But when your flight gets delayed on the tarmac instead of lifting off, or it ends up in a holding pattern […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Tara Friesen

item.title: Bee-made propolis boosts an antifungal drug against yeast pathogens in lab tests
item.description: Propolis may not only inhibit the growth of certain fungi but also affect the activity of drugs used to treat fungal infections. Researchers have investigated how an ethanolic extract of Polish propolis interacts with various antifungal agents. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Banking patterns could help identify people experiencing financial abuse, UK study finds
item.description: Telltale signs of financial abuse, such as depleted savings, increasing debts and declining credit scores, can be identified in bank records, according to an analysis of U.K. banking data published in Nature. The findings reveal up to 373 indicators of financial behavior that could help pinpoint customers who may be experiencing economic abuse. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Central surface density of dark matter agrees with the prediction of a new theory of gravity
item.description: A researcher from Sejong University has used a new theory of gravity proposed by Erik Verlinde to predict the observed central surface density of dark matter. The study was published in Physics of the Dark Universe on Sept. 20. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Aiming at number 9: CASPAR targets fluorine in new science run
item.description: The Compact Accelerator System for Performing Astrophysical Research (CASPAR) recreates conditions inside stars to study how elements are made. The experiment recently restarted with a new target—the ninth element on the periodic table, fluorine. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The Antarctic's only two flowering plants reveal opposing strategies for surviving long-term warming
item.description: A team of Chilean and Spanish researchers has published the results of one of the longest-running in-situ warming experiments in maritime Antarctica in the journal Physiologia Plantarum. The experiment exposed the Antarctic continent's only two native vascular plant species, Deschampsia antarctica (Antarctic hairgrass) and Colobanthus quitensis (Antarctic pearlwort), to passive warming chambers (Open Top Chambers, OTCs) for seven years. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Graphene measurements reveal energy-loss and quantum-coherence exponents diverge under gate control
item.description: Scientists have shown that the two exponents (inelastic scattering exponent and dephasing exponent) commonly used to describe electron scattering in graphene do not necessarily follow the same behavior. Using gated epitaxial graphene, a multi-institutional team of researchers independently extracted the two exponents through current-heating measurements and weak-localization analysis. The contrasting gate-voltage dependence provides evidence that energy relaxation and loss of quantum phase coherence can be governed by different microscopic processes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Evolved enzymes build tuberculosis antibiotic ingredient in the desired form, potentially reducing waste
item.description: Tuberculosis, or TB, is a contagious bacterial infection that primarily affects the lungs. While curative treatments exist, more than 80% of cases occur in low- and middle-income nations, where drug-resistant strains are on the rise and the cost of medications is a burden. A new class of antibiotics has shown promise against multidrug- and extensively drug-resistant TB, but its manufacturing cost is a barrier to access in poorer countries that need the treatments most. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New AI methodology powers the latest million dollar list
item.description: New research from Indiana University Lilly Family School of Philanthropy examines charitable gifts of $1 million or more from 2021 to 2023. The Million-Dollar-Plus Giving in the United States, 2021–2023 report offers insights into how these donors responded to a rapidly changing environment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient genome function persists despite frequent mutations, centromere study shows
item.description: Every time a cell divides, its chromosomes must be distributed correctly between the two daughter cells. Central to this process is the centromere, a specialized region of the chromosome. The centromere serves as the attachment site for the cellular machinery that pulls the chromosomes apart. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Welcomes Croatia as Newest Artemis Accords Signatory
item.description: The Republic of Croatia became the 74th signatory to the Artemis Accords on Wednesday during a ceremony in the capital city of Zagreb with NASA and U.S. Department of State officials present. “It is my privilege to welcome the Republic of Croatia as the latest signatory of the Artemis Accords,” said NASA Deputy Matt Anderson […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Cooling investments in apparel factories can pay for themselves, study shows
item.description: Investing in cooling for Bangladesh's apparel factories can be commercially viable, with an average payback period of one to four years, according to new research from Cornell University's Global Labor Institute (GLI). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists build world's most accurate atomic clock
item.description: Take a second and turn it into trillions of moments. Measure each one. That's how precisely an atomic clock at Singapore's Centre for Quantum Technologies (CQT) keeps time—and with record-setting accuracy, according to results published in Nature on Sept. 23. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Selects Far-Infrared Telescope as First in New Mission Class
item.description: NASA announced Wednesday a mission to explore the history and evolution of the universe, PRIMA (PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics), is advancing to the next phase of development. This space telescope is the first in a new class of NASA astrophysics missions, called Probe Explorers, within the agency’s longstanding Explorers Program. “The PRIMA mission is […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Taveau

item.title: Fluorescence timing identifies eight proteins in one cell with a single staining step
item.description: An international collaboration led by the University Medical Center Göttingen (UMG), Germany, has developed a labeling method that distinguishes fluorescent labels not by color but by how long it takes a dye to emit fluorescence. This makes it possible to visualize eight different proteins in a cell simultaneously in a single step using standard microscopes. The results have been published in the journal ACS Nano. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Political shifts may shape how quickly Germany adopts electric cars and solar power
item.description: A new study conducted by the Climate Action Research Lab (CARL) at the University of Freiburg finds that electric cars and photovoltaic systems are less widespread on average in municipalities with strong support for Alternative for Germany (AfD). The researchers also examined how changes in political support within the same municipalities over time affect subsequent adoption of these technologies. They found that an increase in the AfD's share of the vote is followed by relatively slower adoption of electric cars and photovoltaic systems. The technologies continue to spread, but at a slower… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Prefer intricate shapes? You may also favor complex melodies
item.description: A shape can be considered complex because it has many sides. A complex melody may feature varied pitches and rhythms. Does the mind treat these as separate features, or can it recognize something common beneath their differences? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Unevenness of global warming: Regional warming speedups emerge in waves
item.description: New research from the University of California, Santa Cruz, in collaboration with other institutions, highlights the fragmented and staggered timing of warming increases across the planet, providing a nuanced perspective on the debate over global-warming acceleration. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Palette versus palate: Wine drinkers embrace a spectrum of wine colors
item.description: When a glass of red wine arrives at the table, most drinkers make a snap judgment before taking a sip. Is the color deep enough? Does the hue suggest quality or raise a red flag? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study reveals how biological echo chambers form—and what can break them
item.description: Tropical army ants are known to form devastating armadas that march through forests eating other insects and small creatures. As they march, they deposit chemical trails of pheromones that others behind them sense and follow. But occasionally one of these ants will walk in a circle, prompting a subset of ants behind them to follow until they all collapse and die. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Aircraft to Make Low-Altitude Research Flights Over Colorado
item.description: Agricultural emissions represent an important and understudied part of Earth’s land and atmosphere systems. The FarmFlux mission will deploy more than a dozen sensors to measure ozone, methane, ammonia, particulates, and other pollutants rising from agricultural lands and animal farms and the interaction with the Earth’s atmosphere. The mission is jointly led by NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland; Colorado […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Gianine Figliozzi

item.title: Earth shifted among five 'mega-climate' states over 539 million years, with extinctions spiking near transitions
item.description: Earth's climate has undergone dramatic changes throughout its history, but new research suggests those changes may not have been as random as previously thought. A study led by an international team of researchers, including University of New Mexico paleobiologist Corinne "Cori" Myers, found that Earth's climate over the past 539 million years tended to remain within a small number of recurring climate states. The research also found that periods of elevated extinction, including the five major mass extinction events in Earth's history, frequently occurred as the planet transitioned between… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA's Hubble seeks lensed supernova, marks 200,000 orbits
item.description: NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope completed its 200,000th orbit around Earth on Sept. 19, marking another new milestone for an observatory that continues to transform our understanding of the universe. Hubble has traveled more than 5 billion miles around Earth over its 36-year lifetime, exceeding 1.7 million total observations. An observation completed on the day of […] Publicado también por: NASA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Hubble Telescope Reaches Milestone, Looks for Elusive Supernova
item.description: NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope captured this image of massive galaxy cluster MACS J0417 (left of center) on Sept. 19, 2026. This galaxy cluster acts as a gravitational lens, bending and magnifying light from objects far behind it. Supernova Athena, discovered by NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope in 2025, is predicted to reappear between now and […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: HQ Web Team

item.title: Making sense of shallow-water waves with advanced statistics
item.description: When ocean waves reach shallow water, their complex interactions can produce lower-frequency infragravity waves. These waves strongly affect—and are affected by—the shape of coastlines, linking them to erosion, sediment deposition and the degradation of coastal ice. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Natural compound from soil bacteria offers new approach to treating drug-resistant tuberculosis
item.description: According to the World Health Organization (WHO), more than 10 million people contract tuberculosis (TB) each year. It is one of the deadliest infectious diseases worldwide. Treatment is lengthy and typically involves a combination of several antibiotics over many months. Drug-resistant strains are particularly problematic because the antibiotics used against them are only partially effective. New compounds capable of overcoming existing resistance are urgently needed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Reinvestigation of 6,800-year-old site in Serbia reveals larger settlement and egalitarian social structure
item.description: Southeastern Europe and the Balkans are a key region for understanding the European Neolithic. Many ways of life and economic systems that continue to shape our lives today first emerged there in Europe and later spread across the continent. An archaeological culture named after the Vinča site in present-day Serbia marks a late phase of the Neolithic period in the region. More than 6,500 years ago, people there lived in large settlements for extended periods for the first time. They maintained extensive trade networks. Pottery and stonework demonstrate extensive knowledge of materials and a… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: It's the small things: Treating something as even slightly significant affects motivation
item.description: When Fan Yang's children came home complaining about a crafting class, they had a particularly strong advocate. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Soil heterogeneity helps bacteria find nutrients
item.description: Microorganisms regulate key processes in soils and aquifers, including nutrient cycling, carbon turnover and contaminant degradation. Many bacteria use chemotaxis, the ability to sense and swim toward chemical signals, to locate nutrient-rich hotspots. However, natural subsurface environments are highly heterogeneous, containing complex pore networks that create strong variations in fluid flow and nutrient availability. How these physical conditions influence bacterial foraging has remained poorly understood. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Workers with psychological capital are better prepared to weather increasing work stress
item.description: Workers in the U.S. are feeling the strain of stress and economic uncertainty, and nearly two in five U.S. workers (37%) believe their work environment has a negative impact on their mental health—up from 32% last year, according to the American Psychological Association's 2026 Work in America survey. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Uncovering gravity's impact on the human genome
item.description: The Human Genome Project was launched in 1990, preceded by decades of breakthroughs in genetics. It eventually gave us a sequence of the human genome. Yet, while the physical rules behind the genome's organization remain an active area of research, many questions are still largely unanswered. Among these is the impact of an omnipresent force influencing life on Earth: gravity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The far side of the moon provides clues to a past magnetic field
item.description: Unlike Earth, the moon no longer has a core-generated magnetic field. On our planet, the movement of liquid iron in the outer core generates a global magnetic field. This so-called geodynamo works on a similar principle to a bicycle dynamo, which converts mechanical motion into electrical energy. "Today, there is an ongoing heated debate as to whether the moon also operated a dynamo in the past," says Xi Yang, a Ph.D. student in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at ETH Zurich. This is because analyses of rock samples brought back to Earth by the Apollo astronauts are… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Brain organoids uncover how primates develop different brain shapes
item.description: Most primate species have relatively large brains with surfaces marked by pronounced bulges and furrows. This is not the case with common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus). The brains of these small monkeys are smooth and virtually unfolded. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Kibble with microbial proteins appeals to cats and dogs in new study
item.description: In a new study, cats and dogs showed a short-term preference for kibble containing some protein derived from microorganisms over kibble containing only standard animal-derived protein. Ally Motta de Matos and A.L.B. Cruz of MicroHarvest—an European company that produces protein ingredients through fermentation, with pet food as its first market—present these findings in the open-access journal PLOS One. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A horse named Pea is first to test focused ultrasound treatment of skin tumors called sarcoids
item.description: There is no "one-fix-for-all" solution for sarcoids, said Sophie Bogers, an assistant professor of large animal surgery. Many require chemotherapy or invasive surgery. But she wants a better solution. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hormone-disrupting chemicals found in range of natural and drinking water sources
item.description: A new study has found that chemicals that can affect fertility and reproductive health are contaminating natural and drinking water supplies. The researchers involved in the study have also developed a tool to help detect them. They analyzed samples from natural waterways, tap water, bottled water, tank water and rainwater and found hormone-disrupting substances—estrogenic endocrine-disrupting chemicals—in many of them. The research is published in the journal iScience. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: $100 Pocket Muon Detector: Students build handheld CosmicWatch; sparks citizen-science network
item.description: CosmicWatch is a compact and affordable particle detector that can be used for research and education purposes. Developed by physicist Spencer Axani, it costs about $100 and can be assembled easily. The portable device detects muons, allowing students to investigate cosmic-ray interactions and environmental changes. Researchers have successfully utilized it in high-altitude experiments and various scientific studies. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Exercise keeps astronauts' hearts strong enough for flight to Mars
item.description: Intense exercise during long spaceflights helps maintain heart structure and function within a range needed to tolerate the low-gravity environment of Mars, a study co-led by a UT Southwestern Medical Center researcher suggests. The findings, published in Circulation, not only address an issue critical to future space missions but could also lead to better interventions to improve heart health on Earth. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Variations in virus tails may help predict which phages kill more bacterial strains
item.description: Bacteriophages—or phages, for short—are viruses that kill bacteria, and scientists have been studying them for decades as a possible solution to antibiotic-resistant infections. But phages are notoriously picky eaters—a phage that can eradicate one bacterial strain is often powerless against others, even if the bacteria are closely related. This means a phage that works for one patient may be useless for the next. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Facial recognition trial by police in Australia delivered strong results. But was it an ethical success?
item.description: The results of Australia's first live facial recognition trial have been released. Since June 2026, the Western Australian Police Force has been testing the technology across metropolitan and regional WA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Arctic Sea Ice Reaches 2026 Annual Minimum Extent
item.description: Arctic sea ice reached its annual minimum extent on Sept. 12, according to NASA and the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) at the University of Colorado Boulder. The ice covered an estimated 1.78 million square miles (4.6 million square kilometers), tying 2008, 2010, and 2025 for the 10th-lowest minimum in the satellite record. […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Former NASA chief sounds alarm on China's lunar "exploration" plans
item.description: "Beijing's intended strategy is to dominate the high ground of the twenty-first century." Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Eric Berger

item.description: It's helpful to remember that the view depicted in this image is based on electromagnetic radiation that cannot be seen with the unaided human eye. Dennis Enderson Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Tic-tac-toe simulator offers a way to teach quantum physics without matrix algebra
item.description: A team from SUNY Polytechnic Institute has designed a quantum rule-based simulator known as Quantum Tic-Tac-Toe. The simulator was originally designed to help students learn abstract concepts in quantum mechanics without using matrix algebra, in a game-like environment. It has rules similar to classical tic-tac-toe but incorporates phenomena from quantum mechanics, such as wavefunction collapse, quantum entanglement and quantum superposition. These concepts are also cornerstones of how quantum computers operate. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Roaming black holes may tell the hidden history of galaxies
item.description: If you want to understand the origins of black holes, Yale astronomers say, you need to look beyond the centers of galaxies and start searching in the nooks and crannies. That's where you'll find the "wanderers"—black holes whose journeys may tell the story of how the first black holes formed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New mining map highlights damage caused by extracting metals for your smartphone
item.description: The most sustainable smartphone is the one you currently own. An estimated 80% of your phone's negative impact on the environment happens before the first minute of use—before it is even unboxed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bizarre new dinosaur with giant claws discovered in China
item.description: It walked on two legs and may have looked like a feathered bear with giant claws. Meet Kayrasaurus changliensis—well, its almost complete skeleton, to be precise. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Germany pledges to phase out fossil fuels for first time with target of 2045
item.description: Campaigners say plan marks notable shift away from oil and gas as previously pledges were only for carbon neutrality Europe’s biggest economy, Germany, has committed to phasing out fossil fuels by 2045, despite fierce debate about its green policies. In a roadmap published on Wednesday , the German government set out for the first time an explicit promise of “transitioning away” from fossil fuels. Previous pledges were only for “carbon neutrality”. Continue reading... Publicado también por: The Guardian - Environment. Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Fiona Harvey Environment editor

item.title: Tilcayo: el felino que la ciencia acaba de identificar en Bolivia
item.description: Un equipo internacional de biólogos ha identificado en los bosques nublados de Los Yungas, en Bolivia, una nueva especie de felino silvestre: el Leopardus tilcayo, conocido localmente como tilcayo. El animal llevaba años bajo cuidado en un refugio de vida silvestre, pero los análisis genéticos confirmaron que pertenecía a un linaje diferente. La investigación también permitió identificar una nueva subespecie en Perú, mientras los científicos tratan de determinar la distribución y el estado de conservación de estos pequeños felinos sudamericanos. Fuente: France 24 - Español.
item.dc:creator: María Clara Calle Aguirre

item.title: Spin waves inside a nano-oscillator imaged for the first time
item.description: For the first time, researchers have directly imaged the magnetization dynamics inside a spin Hall nano-oscillator—a nanoscale device that converts direct current into tunable microwave signals and is a promising building block for energy-efficient wireless communication and brain-inspired computing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: SKA may detect magnetic fields on distant exoplanets
item.description: Studying exoplanets has given astronomers insights into the characteristics that could help them find life beyond Earth. For years, astronomers thought an exoplanet's location in a star's habitable zone was enough to make it an Earth-like world. But some stars are more active than our sun, exposing planets in their habitable zones to far more radiation than Earth receives. Astronomers have increasingly recognized that a planet's magnetic field, which shields Earth from harmful radiation, could be a key characteristic in identifying Earth-like worlds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Shannon Lucid’s Record-Setting Mission Aboard Mir
item.description: Shannon Lucid’s Record-Setting Mission Aboard Mir Three days before returning to Earth, Shannon W. Lucid—who joined NASA in 1978 as one of its first six female astronauts—checked in on wheat growing in the Svet greenhouse aboard the Russian space station Mir. For six months, Lucid lived and worked alongside two Russian cosmonauts conducting life science […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Michele Ostovar

item.title: How diffractive solar sails could stop a killer asteroid at 100 km/s
item.description: Asteroids don't come with a warning label that they might one day hit Earth. While we don't know of any currently on course to do so, we are finding thousands of new ones each year, and there's always a chance that one could. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: DIY filter systems improve air quality in classrooms
item.description: As students return to school and cold and flu season begins, researchers are studying ways to improve indoor air quality and reduce the risk of airborne disease transmission. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Report calls for government to introduce a charge on disposable cups
item.description: Around 2.5 billion single-use cups are used in the U.K. every year, yet fewer than 1% are recycled. They contribute to litter, contaminate recycling streams and increase waste management and street cleaning costs for local authorities and taxpayers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why a healthy seafloor matters for the Earth system
item.description: The seafloor is more than just the ground beneath the sea. Two-thirds of Earth's surface is covered by oceans, which have an average depth of almost 4 kilometers (2.5 miles). For a long time, the seafloor's remoteness protected it from widespread human disturbance. But that is changing: Bottom trawling now reaches depths of around 4,000 meters (13,100 feet) and already disturbs up to 2% of the global seafloor each year. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hunting broadly not responsible for birds declining across Europe, study finds
item.description: Hunting is not the main reason bird populations are declining across Europe, according to new research from University College Dublin in collaboration with the Spanish research institute Instituto de Investigación en Recursos Cinegéticos (IREC). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hairy feet, red eyes: Salish Sea reveals two sea spider species new to science
item.description: If you're swimming in the Salish Sea late at night and feel a skittering along your calves, tiny hairy feet tip-tapping their way higher and higher toward your face, don't worry—it's probably just the stuff of nightmares: hairy-legged, red-eyed sea spiders newly discovered by UBC researchers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why is France's Gen Z turning to Catholicism?
item.description: As France prepares for Pope Leo XIV's visit, a surprising trend has emerged in recent years: the number of baptisms among teenagers and young adults has skyrocketed. More than 21,000 catechumens, those undergoing the period of preparation for baptism into the Christian Church, have been recorded so far in 2026. How can this renewed interest in the Catholic faith be explained? Florence Gaillard reports for France in Focus. Fuente: France 24 - English.
item.dc:creator: Florence GAILLARD

item.description: This galaxy is a little extra.... Ver más It's helpful to remember that the view depicted in this image is based on electromagnetic radiation that cannot be seen with the unaided human eye. Ver más comentarios Dennis Enderson Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Governments across Australia know how to stop violence against Indigenous women, they just don't do it
item.description: Indigenous women and children experience disproportionate levels of family violence. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women are killed at rates up to six times higher than non-Indigenous women, overwhelmingly by intimate partners (76%) or family members. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Adding limestone to Mississippi River Basin farmlands acts as a major carbon sink, study finds
item.description: In a discovery as broad and far-reaching as the Big Muddy itself, a new Yale–led study says farmers in the Mississippi River Basin are storing more carbon dioxide (CO2) in the soil than they emit when they add limestone to their fields, an agricultural practice known as "liming." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How evolution shaped the human skeleton: Clues from cartilage
item.description: Human and chimpanzee genomes are more than 98% identical, and the genes themselves barely differ. The changes that make us human are thought to hide instead in the DNA that controls when and where genes switch on. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New Study Illuminates Bats’ Murky Origins
item.description: The largest analysis of bat genomes and fossils suggests that the first bats emerged in Europe roughly 65 million years ago and that echolocation evolved early. Fuente: The New York Times - World.
item.dc:creator: Emily Anthes

item.title: Bat genomes and fossils point to a European origin 65 million years ago
item.description: New research from the University of St Andrews has created the largest combined study of bat genomes and fossils ever undertaken, finding that bats most likely originated in Europe around 65 million years ago before spreading across the world. Fuente: Phys.org.
